result: HIV's envelope (Env) protein evolves extremely rapidly, with descendants of the pandemic HIV-1 virus now showing as little as 65% protein identity—a level of divergence comparable to that between human and mouse orthologs over 90 million years. This rapid evolution erodes the efficacy of most neutralizing antibodies.
evaluation: Claims C1, C3, C4, and C5 are well-supported by citations to prior literature (Lynch et al., 2009; Waterston et al., 2002; Hedges et al., 2006; Albert et al., 1990; Wei et al., 2003; Richman et al., 2003; Burton et al., 2005). The comparison to human-mouse divergence provides appropriate context for the magnitude of HIV Env evolution.

result: The immediate evolutionary space accessible to HIV Env is defined by single amino acid mutational effects, which can be measured by deep mutational scanning. During evolution, substitutions at one site can change mutational effects at other sites through epistasis, though the magnitude of these shifts is usually limited. Env's structural complexity as a large, heavily glycosylated heterotrimeric complex that transitions through multiple conformational states distinguishes it from proteins previously studied for epistatic shifts.
evaluation: Claims C6-C13 establish the conceptual framework and prior knowledge for the study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Al-Mawsawi et al., 2014; Duenas-Decamp et al., 2016; Haddox et al., 2016; Natarajan et al., 2013; Gong et al., 2013; Harms and Thornton, 2014; and others). The characterization of Env's structural complexity is well-documented.

result: The study uses two transmitted-founder Envs from clade A HIV-1: BG505 (T332N variant) and BF520, which share 86.2% overall identity and 89.1% identity in the mutagenized ectodomain and transmembrane domains. BG505 has been extensively studied structurally and is being tested as a vaccine immunogen, while BF520 was isolated from an infant who developed an early broad antibody response.
evaluation: Claims C22-C27 and C81-C82 describe the viral strains used in the study. The sequence identity calculations (C23, C24) are quantitative data from the study. The characterization of BG505 and BF520 is supported by multiple citations (Nduati et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2006; Goo et al., 2014; Julien et al., 2013; Sanders et al., 2013, 2015; de Taeye et al., 2015; Simonich et al., 2016).

result: The authors developed an improved deep mutational scanning strategy for transmitted-founder Envs, excluding signal peptide and cytoplasmic tail to reduce expression-level effects. Key modifications included using SupT1.CCR5 cells, performing a short high-MOI infection instead of a full second passage, and conducting the experiment in full biological triplicate for both BG505 (670 sites) and BF520 (662 sites).
evaluation: Claims C28, C85-C91 describe the methodological approach. The rationale for excluding signal peptide and cytoplasmic tail is supported by citations (Chakrabarti et al., 1989; Yuste et al., 2004; Li et al., 1994). The use of SupT1.CCR5 cells is supported by citation to Boyd et al., 2015. The experimental design with biological triplicates is clearly documented in Figure 2B.

result: The deep mutational scanning effectively selected for functional Envs, as evidenced by strong purifying selection against stop codons (frequencies dropping to 3-16% of original values) and nonsynonymous mutations (43-49% of original values), while synonymous mutations dropped only slightly (85-95%). This pattern is consistent with nonsynonymous mutations being often deleterious while synonymous mutations have milder effects.
evaluation: Claims C29-C34 describe validation of the experimental selection. The quantitative data (C30-C32) are presented in Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 1. The interpretation (C33-C34) is consistent with established principles of molecular evolution, with C34 supported by citation to Zanini and Neher, 2013.

result: Replicates for each Env are more correlated with each other than with replicates for the other Env, suggesting some shifts in amino acid preferences. There is a trend for highly preferred amino acids to be more strongly preferred in BG505 than BF520, likely reflecting modest differences in experimental stringency rather than inherent differences between Envs.
evaluation: Claims C36-C38 describe observations from Figure 3B and the data analysis. The correlation patterns are clearly visible in the figure, and the interpretation regarding experimental stringency is supported by the stop codon analysis showing stronger purifying selection in BG505 (Figure 3—source data 1).

result: Experimentally informed codon models (ExpCMs) based on deep mutational scanning of either BG505 or BF520 describe natural Env evolution vastly better than standard codon substitution models (Table 1). The gene-wide average omega > 1 for ExpCMs indicates that external selection (e.g., from immunity) drives amino acid fixation faster than expected from functional constraints alone. The stringency parameters > 1 suggest experimental selections were more lax than natural selection.
evaluation: Claims C39, C41, and C44 describe phylogenetic modeling results shown in Table 1. The improved fit of ExpCMs is quantified by AIC values. The interpretation of omega > 1 and stringency parameters is consistent with the ExpCM framework (Hilton et al., 2017; Bloom, 2017) and supported by the stop codon analysis.

result: The amino acid preference maps are consistent with prior knowledge: CD4-binding residues (T257, D368, E370, W427, D457) are highly preferred, cysteines at disulfide bond sites are highly preferred, and most sites in variable loops are mutationally tolerant. This concordance with prior mutational studies and the improved phylogenetic models suggest the experiments authentically measure functional selection on Env.
evaluation: Claims C45-C52 and C67 validate the experimental results against prior knowledge. The CD4-binding residues are supported by citation to Olshevsky et al., 1990; disulfide bonds by van Anken et al., 2008; and variable loops by Starcich et al., 1986 and Zolla-Pazner and Cardozo, 2010. The experimental data (Figures 4 and 5) are consistent with these prior findings, and the improved phylogenetic fit (Table 1) provides additional validation.

result: Most sites show no detectable shifts in amino acid preferences between BG505 and BF520, but 30 sites have clearly shifted preferences (at FDR 0.1). The amino acid preferences of most sites are conserved between these moderately diverged viral strains, and from a qualitative perspective, the preferences look mostly similar. This conservation has useful implications for many purposes.
evaluation: Claims C15, C16, C21, C54, C70, and C71 describe the main finding regarding conservation of amino acid preferences. The identification of 30 shifted sites is based on rigorous statistical analysis (Figure 6B) using a null distribution approach. The conclusion that most sites are conserved is supported by the correlation data (Figure 3B) and the similarity of results between the two Envs (Figure 9C).

result: Shifts in amino acid preferences are only slightly enriched at sites that have substituted between the Envs, and many shifts occur at residues that do not contact substitutions. Only 8 of 30 shifted sites differ in amino acid identity between BG505 and BF520. This lack of strong enrichment contrasts with previous protein-wide experimental and simulation-based studies that found shifts dramatically more pronounced at sites of substitutions.
evaluation: Claims C18, C19, C75, C93-C96 describe a surprising finding about the distribution of shifts. The quantitative data (8 of 30 shifted sites have substituted) is from the analysis in Figure 7D and Figure 7—source data 1. The structural analysis (Figure 7C, D) shows no significant enrichment of shifts at substituted sites or sites contacting substitutions. The contrast with prior work is supported by citations to Doud et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2015.

result: Long-range epistasis can unpredictably shift Env's mutational tolerance during HIV evolution. A subset of sites change markedly in which mutations they tolerate, with some shifted sites simply accommodating more amino acids in the more stable BG505 Env. The majority of shifted sites have the same wild-type amino acid in both Envs despite shifted preferences. Env's exceptional conformational complexity may explain why shifts are not enriched at sites of substitutions, as mutations can cause long-range alterations in Env's conformation.
evaluation: Claims C20, C73, C74, C78, C79, and C97 interpret the findings on epistasis. The observation that most shifted sites have the same wild-type amino acid (C78) is quantified in the data. The hypothesis about conformational complexity (C79, C97) is supported by citations to studies showing mutations cause long-range conformational changes (Kwong et al., 2000; White et al., 2010; Almond et al., 2010; Davenport et al., 2013; Munro et al., 2014; Ozorowski et al., 2017). The comparison to other proteins (C74) is supported by citations.

result: Sites of significant shifts are clustered in the structures of both closed and open Env trimers, with clustering becoming stronger when considering minimum distance across both conformations. There is no significant difference in solvent accessibility between shifted and non-shifted sites. Many shifted sites cluster within conformationally dynamic regions: one cluster at the trimer apex where variable loops pack together, and another near a hydrophobic network that helps transmit conformational changes upon CD4 binding. Nearly half (13 of 30) of shifted sites are in these two clusters.
evaluation: Claims C111-C113 and C98-C103 describe structural analysis of shifted sites. The clustering is statistically demonstrated in Figure 7C. The lack of association with solvent accessibility is shown in Figure 7B. The identification of specific clusters is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2, with the V2 region dynamics supported by citation to Verkerke et al., 2016 and the hydrophobic network by Ozorowski et al., 2017. The quantification (13 of 30 sites) is from the data analysis.

result: BG505 SOSIP is more thermostable than BF520 SOSIP, and sites with altered mutational tolerance are often more mutationally tolerant in BG505. Differences in Env expression level might contribute to broadening or narrowing of mutational tolerance. Some sites, like site 288, flip amino acid preference without altering mutational tolerance.
evaluation: Claims C114-C117 describe patterns in the shifted sites. The thermostability difference (C114) is supported by citations to Binley et al., 2000; Sanders et al., 2002; Verkerke et al., 2016. The observation about mutational tolerance (C115) is from Figure 6C. The hypothesis about expression level (C116) is reasonable speculation given the experimental design. The example of site 288 (C117) is shown in Figure 6C.

result: Analysis of entrenchment shows that the average effect of mutations converting BG505 to BF520 or vice versa is deleterious, though there are substantial exceptions. Even unfavorable inter-Env mutational flips are generally more favorable than random amino acid mutations. Entrenchment occurs for some but not all substitutions distinguishing BG505 and BF520, with magnitude less than a typical random mutation. Entrenchment contributes to some mutational shifts but is not the only cause, as many shifts occur at sites that do not differ between Envs.
evaluation: Claims C104-C110 describe the entrenchment analysis shown in Figure 8. The conceptual framework (C104) is standard. The quantitative observations (C105-C107) are from the data distributions in Figure 8. The conclusions (C108-C110) are well-supported by the data and the observation that many shifted sites have not substituted (Figure 7D).

result: Sites evolving faster or slower than expected are similar regardless of whether BG505 or BF520 experiments are used, suggesting either dataset provides a reasonable approximation of functional constraints across clade A Envs. Most sites of faster-than-expected evolution are on Env's surface. Since deep mutational scanning did not impose antibody pressure, sites where substitutions are antibody-driven will evolve faster in nature than expected from experiments.
evaluation: Claims C53, C55-C58 describe the comparison of experimental and natural selection. The similarity of results between Envs is shown in Figure 9C. The surface location of faster-evolving sites is shown in Figure 9A, B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1. The interpretation regarding antibody-driven evolution (C58) is supported by citation to Moore et al., 2009 and is a logical inference from the experimental design.

result: Immune selection offers a plausible explanation for sites evolving slower than expected. Env employs strategies to reduce antibody susceptibility including glycan shielding and adopting closed conformations. Sites contributing to these immune-evasion strategies are under constraint in nature not present in experiments. Of 21 shared N-linked glycosylation sites, only four are under strong selection in experiments despite most being conserved in nature, consistent with glycans being selected primarily for immune evasion. A network of sites regulating Env's conformational transitions also evolves slower than expected.
evaluation: Claims C59-C66 interpret sites evolving slower than expected. The hypothesis (C59) is reasonable speculation. The immune evasion strategies (C60-C61) are supported by citations (Wei et al., 2003; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Gristick et al., 2016; Kwong et al., 2002; Guttman et al., 2015; Ozorowski et al., 2017). The glycosylation site analysis (C63-C65) is shown in Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2, with interpretation supported by citations (Pugach et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2013; Rathore et al., 2017). The conformational network (C66) is shown in Figure 9D.

result: The study draws an analogy to structural biology: closely homologous proteins have similar structures, and SOSIP trimer structures from diverse Env strains remain highly similar. The authors anticipate the complete maps of mutational effects will be useful for future sequence-structure-function studies and for computationally parameterizing fitness landscapes of Env.
evaluation: Claims C68, C69, C72, and C80 make predictions about future utility. The analogy to structural biology (C68-C69) is well-supported by citations (Chothia and Lesk, 1986; Sander and Schneider, 1991; Julien et al., 2015; Pugach et al., 2015; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Verkerke et al., 2016; Gristick et al., 2016). However, the predictions about future utility (C72, C80) are speculative and cannot be evaluated without follow-up work demonstrating this utility.

result: A prior study of influenza nucleoprotein found significant enrichment of shifts at sites of substitutions, contrasting with the current findings. Although there is some entrenchment of differences between BG505 and BF520, this is not the major factor behind shifts in amino acid preferences.
evaluation: Claims C76 and C77 compare the current findings to prior work. The citation to Doud et al., 2015 (C76) is appropriate. The conclusion about entrenchment (C77) is supported by the data in Figure 8 and the observation that most shifted sites have not substituted.

result: The authors previously created comprehensive codon-mutant libraries of BF520 Env for antibody escape mapping, but these libraries had not been characterized for effects on viral growth prior to this study.
evaluation: Claims C83 and C84 describe prior work. C83 is supported by citation to Dingens et al., 2017. C84 is a statement about what was not done in that prior work, which is verifiable from the cited paper.
